title: Time Passes · 10
paragraphs: Then, truly, peace had come. Breaths of peace, messages of peace, came from the sea to the shore: never again to disturb its sleep, but to lull it into a deeper rest, and to confirm whatever the dreamers dreamed, in holiness and wisdom—what else could it be murmuring?—as Lily Briscoe laid her head on the pillow in the clean, quiet room and listened to the sea. In through the open window came the voice of the world’s beauty, murmuring too softly for its exact words to be made out—but what did that matter, if the meaning was clear? It pleaded with the sleepers (the house was full once more; Mrs. Beckwith was staying, and Mr. Carmichael as well) that if they would not actually come down to the beach, they should at least raise the blind and look out. Then they would see night flowing down in purple, his head crowned, his scepter set with jewels, and how a child might gaze into his eyes. And if they still held back (Lily, worn out by the journey, fell asleep almost at once, but Mr. Carmichael read a book by candlelight)—if they still refused, saying that this splendor of his was mere vapor, that the dew was stronger than he was, and that they would rather sleep—then the voice would sing its song gently, without complaint or argument. The waves would break gently (Lily heard them as she slept); the light fell tenderly (it seemed to come to her through her eyelids). And it all looked, thought Mr. Carmichael, closing his book and drifting off, very much the way it had looked years ago.

The voice might well take up its plea again, as the curtains of darkness folded themselves over the house, over Mrs. Beckwith, Mr. Carmichael and Lily Briscoe, until they lay with many layers of blackness pressed on their eyes. Why not accept this? Why not be content with it, yield, and be resigned? The sighing of all the seas breaking in rhythm around the islands soothed them; night wrapped them round; nothing disturbed their sleep. Then the birds started up, and dawn wove their thin voices into its whiteness; a cart went grinding by; somewhere a dog barked; the sun lifted the curtains and tore the veil from their eyes. And Lily Briscoe, stirring as she slept, clutched at her blankets the way a person falling clutches at the turf at the edge of a cliff. Her eyes flew open. So here she was again, she thought, sitting bolt upright in bed. Awake.
